title: The constitution
description: The order of the religion: its head, its law, its offices.
html:
Read in the Ide dialect. The original is written in Igbo; here the one term that changes is chi → si, Ide has chi: it is the word, and si / sị is how it is widely said. Nothing here is rewritten — the documents stand as written.

The Constitution of Odiana

The order of the religion: one head, one law, one canon, one order of temples.

Odiana is a central religion, and its shape is deliberate: one supreme head, a college of diocesan heads under him, districts between them and the temples, a parish temple in every community with a school and a healing house beside it, one cathedral, one vault, one law, one canon, one calendar, and a graded lay order. That is the architecture of a central church, built in Igbo terms and on the institutions of the Igbo.

Every rule is marked inherited, reformed or invented, and every claim names its source.

1 · What Odiana is

Odiana is the religion of the Ide people, grown from the religion of the Igbo. It takes the substance of Odinani and the machinery of the old order, and gathers them under a single head.

Its own summary of itself:

Law is Ana. Interpretation is afa. Enforcement is the community and the spirits.

The authority, in order: the author's decisions → this constitution → the canon (Obibi Nso) → the purity code and the temple code → the liturgy.

What is inherited, and what is new

| | | |---|---| | inherited from Igbo religion | Chukwu, the alusi, chi, Ana, the ancestors, afa, nso, alu, ikpu alu, ofo, the four market days, the moral law | | held in the old Igbo order | the Ndose as a temple, the council, Nze na Ozo as a graded body, the eze ana, the licence regime, isube nso, Igu Aro, the four-part judiciary, the taboo ladder | | reformed | no blood on an altar or a shrine, and no blood brought to any holy thing — while an animal is killed at every festival and serious rite, in the open; cleanliness as a standing doctrine; permanent, maintained temples; the reform promulgated by iwu | | Odiana's own | the single headship (Ikala), the diocesan structure (Isiala, Eze Ana, Okwu-Ana, Ndose), the cathedral (Obuchukwu), the vault (Uneri), the school and healing house attached to every temple, the canon Obibi Nso, and the festival calendar |

And the honesty that has to come first: the old ritual order was abolished. Its reach was widest around the thirteenth to the late seventeenth century, declined, and was ended by force in 1911 — its king desecrated, and its own ritual power of abrogating taboo turned against it in front of the assembled towns. Odiana keeps the old institutions, and it does not pretend to restore the old order.

2 · The supreme level

Ikala — the head of Odiana

ikala, from okala mmadụ, okala mmụọ — half human, half spirit. The supreme spiritual authority of the religion, and its guardian. His authority is absolute, and it is not shared.

What he holds: the law of Ana; the balance of Chukwu, Ana and mankind; the ofo of the religion; the confirmation of every Eze Ana; the licensing of every temple and every priest; and the announcement of the year.

He does not sacrifice. In the old order: "After the coronation of the old head, which involved his 'death' and 'resurrection', he is regarded as a spirit. He does not offer sacrifices because sacrifices are offered to spirits, which he is believed to be… He appoints a chief priest to be in charge of all rituals." So the head appoints the officiant and does not officiate. In Odiana, where no blood is brought to the altar, that separation is complete.

He is not a chief priest. "The the old head is not a chief priest and does not perform the function of a chief priest generally ascribed to him by casual observers." His work is to authorise, to licence, to judge and to cleanse.

How he is chosen: hereditary, from the royal lineage, and confirmed publicly by the college of Eze Ana — as the old order's head was "ritually inspired" rather than elected.

And he is not above correction. See §10.

There is no second-in-command

This is deliberate, and it is the first thing to understand about the shape of Odiana. The head holds "the abrogation of any taboo" alone, and a religion that invents a deputy invents a rival. So no office in Odiana outranks another, and none of them sits in his seat.

What stands beneath him is three offices and two bodies — and they are not a ladder. A man may hold one, and answer to the Ikala directly, and to nobody else.

| the office | holds | |---|---| | Idenze — the head of the state council | he speaks with the head's voice. He carries the Ikala's word, oversees the works of the religion and its dealings abroad, and answers for its fabric and its goods. He holds no rank above any other, and he is appointed, not elected — and his office ends the moment the Ikala dies. He is the head's hand, and a hand is not a successor | | Alo — the custody of the house | held by the Iyi. While the Ikala lives she holds the sacred things — the reserve ofo, the register, the seal, and the vault Uneri. The moment the Ikala dies she becomes the administrator of the whole religion until a successor is confirmed. She is the only person in Odiana whose authority grows at the head's death | | Ndi Ikenye — the heads of the works | each great work has a head, and each answers to the Ikala alone: the law (Iwu) · the purity code (Ịdị Ọcha) · the calendar and the festivals (Emume) · the priesthood and its licensing (Ọkwa) · the schools (Unako) · the healing houses (Edem) · the vault (Uneri) · and afa |

| the body | is | |---|---| | Nzemabua | the council of state. It advises the head on the law, on the calendar and on the great matters, and it cannot command him. the Igbo name: "Offences are brought to the court of the Nzemabua council, which discusses the nature and character of the taboos." | | the college of Eze Ana | every diocesan head together. It elects the next Ikala, and it confirms him. This is the body with the seat, and it is a body and not a man |

And every one of those names is the old order's, and not this book's. The monograph of the old order records the offices themselves, and the religion takes the names with them:

  • isi nze — "The head of all the ozo men is called isi nze, head of nze-titled men." And it is he who

announces a decision: "only the ozo men will make the decision and the isi nze announces it." Where a lineage has no ozo men, "the ikenye okolobia will make the decision and the head of the ikenye okolobia will make the announcement."

  • isi nzemabua — "The leader of this group, also, is the first amongst them to take the ozo title, and is

called isi nzemabua. The man who is the isi nzemabua is also the isi ndi nze, although he plays different roles in the two councils." So the head of the council and the head of the titled men are one man, and he is not above the head of the religion — "The ultimate head is the the old head."

  • alo — "the custodian of the temple. The alo is the staff…" The name Odiana gives to the custody is

the name of the staff that carries it, and it is the Iyi who holds it.

  • ikenye okolobia, also called ndi ichie nta — "all the non-ozo elders, ikenye okolobia; and all the

other younger men, umu okolobia." They are the leaders of the men who hold no title, and Odiana gives them the works — so that the religion's business is not held only by its titled men.

  • umu okolobia and the age-grades, whose isi ogbo heads them — and they are the ones who

execute what the council decides: "The age-grades of the lineage will then execute the decision."

  • And okpala, "inheritor and custodian" of a lineage's temple — the firstborn who holds the ground.

In Odiana the custodian holds the ground and the priest holds the office, and the two are not the same man unless the lineage chooses it.

'The leader is the adviser of the group and derives the authority to lead from accepted traditional sources.' That sentence is the whole of what Odiana means by an office, and it is why no office in this religion outranks another: authority here is not taken from a seat. It is granted by the people who are sitting.

And the rule that holds them together: no office above another, and none in the head's seat. The Mouth does not outrank the Keeper; the Keeper does not outrank the heads of the works; and all of them answer to the college when the seat is empty.

Iyi — the female head

She is not the Ikala's equal, and she is the most powerful person in the religion after him. Both halves of that sentence are the ruling, and neither may be dropped.

What she holds:

  • Alo — the custody of the house. The sacred things while the Ikala lives, and the

administration of the whole religion when he dies.

  • the women's order, and everything that belongs to it;
  • the fertility rites, and the purity of marriage and childbirth;
  • Unako and Edem — the school and the healing house are the women's, and a man does not head

them (§11);

  • a seat in the council in her own right;
  • and she does not bow or kneel before any human being. Not before the Ikala, and not before the

college.

And she holds no Ndose. The Iyi is never the head of a temple and never the priest of a parish, and no Ndose is hers. Her authority does not come from a temple — it comes from the women's order, from Unako and Edem, and from Alo, the seat that runs the religion when the head dies. The men have the temple. The women have the house, the school and the keeping — and the woman who holds all three does not need a Ndose to be the most powerful person after the Ikala.

How she is chosen. The college of Eze Ana elects her, and it confirms her — the same body that elects and confirms the Ikala. The two heads are raised by one college, and the difference between them is not how they are raised but what they hold.

Why she is not his equal. The Ikala holds the ofo of the religion and the abrogation of taboo; she does not. A matter of doctrine, a new iwu, and the confirmation of a diocese are his; the house, the school, the healing, the women's order, and the seat that is filled when he dies are hers. The religion gave the woman the one thing a head cannot have: she outlives the vacancy.

Her ladder is a real ladder, attested in the old order: inyom → Umokpu → ilimmadunato → Nne Mmau, "the greatest honour a lineage can give to a woman", which "gives the woman some of the privileges of a male citizen."

And she may hold the Ika Dibia as of right — see §11.

One honest limit: admitting women to Ozo itself is attested nowhere — the women's ladder ends where the men's begins. Odiana keeps the parallel ladder and does not open Ozo, and says so rather than implying a reform it has not made.

3 · The diocesan level

Isiala — a diocese · Isi + Ana

The highest territorial unit of the religion. Each Isiala holds:

  • one central Ndose — the Obuchukwu of that diocese;
  • the afa authority of the territory;
  • a court for the law of Ana;
  • a network of Ndose — its parishes.

Eze Ana — the head of a diocese

The supreme authority within an Isiala, and the chief interpreter of the divine will through afa. His office:

  • he oversees every Dibia and Dibia in the diocese;
  • he holds doctrinal interpretation — the book of afa;
  • he enforces morality — the law of Ana and of Amadioha;
  • he presides over the major rites and judgements;
  • and his legitimacy is confirmed by the Ikala.

The college of Eze Ana — every diocesan head together — is the body that advises the Ikala, and the body that confirms him.

4 · The district level

Okwu-Ana — a deanery

A group of Ndose in a district, standing between the diocese and the parish. Its work is uniformity: that the rite is done the same way in every temple of the district, and that the law is enforced the same way.

Its head is the Isiafa — the deacon, who licenses the priests of his district and answers to the Eze Ana.

5 · The parish level

Ndose — a temple, and a parish

The living centre of Ana, and the unit of the religion that a person actually belongs to. Every Ndose carries:

| with it | is | |---|---| | Edem | the healing house: herbs, water, rest, and the care of the body | | Unako | the school: the law, the purity code, the calendar and the tradition | | Obu | the home of the priests — the dwelling of the priests who serve the Ndose. It stands inside the Ndose compound, or beside it, or near it: the priests live at the temple they serve |

And inside it: the threshold and the washing place · the swept court · the bloodless altar · the inner room · the place of divination · the ancestral place. See temple.md.

Ika Dibia — the chief priest of a Ndose

He leads all ritual activity in the parish, and heads every Dibia in it. He answers to the Eze Ana. He runs and controls the Ndose, and he is the one office in the religion that is reserved. See below.

The four orders beneath him

| order | is | |---|---| | Dibia Ana | the custodian of the earth: cleansing, the purification of land, and cases of nso and alu | | Dibia Afa | the diviner; the closest to doctrinal authority under the Eze Ana | | Dibia Agwu | the calling, the inspiration, and the states that come with them | | Dibia Ogwu | the healer, working through the Edem |

Who may hold an order — the ruling

A woman may hold every order in this religion, and each is conferred on her exactly as on a man. Dibia Afa, Dibia Ogwu, Dibia Agwu, Dibia Ana — all of them are hers to hold, and there is no order beneath the Ika Dibia that is closed to her.

And one office is reserved.

| the office | who holds it | |---|---| | the Ika Dibia | reserved to men. In rare cases a woman may hold it — where she has attained a high level of spirituality — and in that case it is the diocesan council that confers it, and not the Eze Ana alone and not the parish. And the Iyi may hold it as of right |

Why the reservation, and why the exception. The Ika Dibia runs and controls the Ndose — the house of the men. The religion divides the two houses and gives each its own head: the Ndose is led by men, and Edem and Unako are led by women, and a man does not head the healing house or the school any more than a woman heads the temple. The exception is not a loophole. It is the recognition that spirituality is not a sex, and that a woman who has climbed further than the men around her is not to be stopped at a door by the accident of her body.

And the two heads of the two houses are not above one another. The Iyi is not the Ika Dibia's superior, and he is not hers. They answer to the Eze Ana in their own spheres, and both answer to the Ikala.

And both houses are in the council, and neither outranks the other there.

The works of the two houses, in full:

| the women's house | the men's house | |---|---| | Unako — the school: the teaching of the law, the purity code, the calendar and the tradition, and the teaching of reading and number besides | the Ndose — the temple, the assembly, the offering and the rites | | Edem — the healing house: herbs, water, the care of the body, and the cure | the licensing of priests, and the register of the parish | | the women's order, and its ladder — inyom, Umokpu, ilimmadunato, Nne Mmau | the titled body — Nze na Ozo, §8 | | the fertility rites, and the purity of marriage and childbirth | the law, and the courts, §9 | | the keeping of the house — Alo, the sacred things and the seal | the announcing of the year — Igu Aro |

And neither house is a demotion. The religion does not rank the school below the temple, and it does not rank the healing house below the altar. A Ndose without its Edem and its Unako is not a Ndose.

6 · The cathedral, and the vault

Obuchukwu — the cathedral · obi + Chukwu

The central Ndose of a diocese, and the religion's own seat at the head town. Its chief priest is the Ika Mmuo — the same dignity as an Ika Dibia, at the cathedral.

Uneri — the vault

One only, at the cathedral of the religion, and served by the guild of the sacred arts rather than by the priesthood. It holds the lineage relics — the remains taken at burial and worked into the designated lineage artefact — and it is the religion's memory of its dead.

7 · The council

The governing body beside the head, and it follows the old order's:

| body | is | |---|---| | the council | the appellate court for taboo, the body that announces the year, and the body that confirms the head. It sits with the Iyi in her own right | | the college of Eze Ana | the diocesan heads, who advise and confirm | | the titled body | Nze na Ozo, §8 | | the deacons | the Isiafa of each Okwu-Ana |

the Igbo words for what such a council decides: "Offences are brought to the court of the Nzemabua council, which discusses the nature and character of the taboos."

What the council does not decide: the day-to-day government of any town or lineage. See §9.

8 · The lay order — Nze na Ozo

The graded body of the religion, taken and not given. Ozo is not hereditary; it is achieved and paid for, and open to men who meet the requirements.

The rungs below Ozo are three — Ima Mmau at about nine · Ichi, with its six stages · Nli Nwammadu, the novitiate, gated on marriage. Ozo itself is a nine-stage sequence, ending in twenty-one days' seclusion and the public confession and entry in the register.

Rank is a set of obligations, not a set of honours. the old order's ladder, with its shares of the population:

| stratum | share | own taboos | |---|---|---| | the head | 0.1% | yes | | Ozo / ndị nze | 2.4% | yes | | okolobia — grown men without Ozo | 19.0% | yes | | married women, inyom | 21.5% | yes | | children — "ritual minors" | 57.0% | the only exempt stratum |

And the annual public confession is the engine of it — a titled man declares his wrongs before the community each year, "enforced by belief that concealment brings immediate illness followed by a disgraceful death."

And the mandate of the body is one sentence: to admit, to enforce correct payment and ritual, to run the market under the ofo staff, to distribute dividends, and to police the rules.

9 · The law

iwu is not nso

"The the old head and his councils make laws to be obeyed by the whole of the old order. An infraction of these laws

does not constitute breaking a taboo. Those who break the laws are punished or fined."

| | iwu | nso | |---|---|---| | what it is | enacted law — made by the head and the council | taboo — inherited, and not made by anyone | | breach | punished or fined | defilement, requiring cleansing | | how it changes | repealed or amended | promulgated or abrogated, by isube nso |

Odiana legislates by iwu. Every change to practice is promulgated as enacted law — published, dated and recorded — and never presented as a recovered taboo. The power to abrogate is the head's: "He alone can order the abrogation of any taboo or pronounce the enactment of new ones" — and it is exercised publicly, in front of the assembled, which is how the old order's reform was meant to work, and how it was turned against the old order in 1911.

The courts

| court | hears | |---|---| | the Ndose | minor matters | | the Isiala | major cases, escalated | | the district, through the Isiafa | uniformity, and the disputes within it | | the council | the nature and character of a taboo — the appellate court | | the assembly | the greatest matters: forty-nine elders, seven times seven, and "the minority, even if wrong, must be heard for three days." |

And only a licensed priest may cleanse — the old order's rule that purification is done by "specially authorized persons".

The offences and the remedies

| offence | remedy | |---|---| | theft | restitution fourfold | | injury | not retaliation — the offender works the victim's farm for a full planting season | | murder | not death — banishment and the blood-price | | moving a sacred boundary stone | the stone returned, and the wound sealed | | incest | the union is a lost echo: it cannot inherit | | a false oath on the ofo | banishment until public confession | | poverty | alu — "Poverty is disorder, not virtue." |

And the law restores rather than avenges. "Justice is not about revenge; it is about restoring the broken circle of the community."

And the guilt is shared — the heaviest doctrine in the religion: "When someone commits nso, it affects the whole community; and if the crime is severe enough, entire groups and everyone would be held responsible." That is why the remedy is public, and why the cleansing must be one a whole community can perform.

10 · The head is not infallible — a deliberate departure

the old order held the opposite, and Odiana records the departure rather than copying it:

"the old order people believe that he does not err. It is the Nzemabua who take all the blame and public

criticism."

The consequence the source itself draws: the old order tradition contains no account of a bad head — not because there were none, but because the record could not hold one.

Odiana does not keep this. The Ikala is not doctrinally incapable of error. His office is sacred; his judgement is not. The council may be wrong and be corrected, the amendments in canon.md may be revised, and a document that cannot report its own failures has stopped being useful.

11 · The licence regime — how the centre governs

This is the Igbo machinery.

"Before 1911 … no-one dared make an Alusi, or rebuild its temple or transfer its temple to another spot

without permission from the old head. The chief priests of these Alusi were directly controlled from the old order."

The centre licenses four things, and Odiana keeps all four:

| licensed | in Odiana | |---|---| | the creation of a deity | no new alusi is constituted without the Ikala's licence | | the building of its temple | no Ndose is built without a licence | | the relocation of its temple | a Ndose does not move without one | | the appointment of its priest | every priest is licensed from the centre |

The instrument is ofo and alo — authority from the ancestors and power from Chukwu. And the distinction is the Igbo:

"Power to act on people, in the old order thinking, is of divine origin while authority to use power is of social

origin."

So no office in Odiana holds power — only the authority to use it, and authority can be withdrawn.

And the regime reached to the smallest offering. Without ofo and alo from the the old order priest, a local monarch was "unable even to offer kola-nuts to the tribal gods" — so even a bloodless offering required central authorisation. The licence is what makes an offering valid.

12 · The limit — the religion, not the state

"This system of control of settlements did not involve control over day-to-day running of the

government of settlements. Each settlement managed its internal affairs according to its customs and

traditions. Only matters related to taboos and abominations, the interpretation of customs and

traditions, long standing disputes within the towns or between the towns were submitted to the old head."

So Odiana centralises its worship, its calendar, its licensing and its jurisprudence of taboo — and nothing else. It is a religion, not a government.

13 · The year

The week is four days — Eke, Orie, Afo, Nkwo — and the days are persons, not numbers.

The year is announced, not computed locally: the old order's ran "according to the calculation made and announced by the Ndi Nze, a state council", in Igu Aro. So the council publishes the calendar and no Ndose sets its own. The tradition computes the dates from lunations.

And the year is gendered: the old order's ritual calendar carries "OFFERING TO MEN'S CHI" and "OFFERING TO WOMEN'S CHI" as separate entries — the calendar warrant for the dual headship of §2.

14 · Membership

Rank in Odiana is the set of obligations you carry, not the honours you hold — the Igbo principle, and the most useful thing it gives a modern religion, because it makes standing something you take on rather than something you are born into.

So rank is achieved, not ascribed. The ladder is earned and paid for; it is not a caste. Odiana has no caste. Birth determines no one's standing, and no office is closed by birth except the lineage of the Ikala itself.

And a person belongs to a Ndose, which keeps their name registered — the identity the rites require.

15 · Still open — for the author

| # | the question | |---|---| | 1 | How many Isiala there are, and where their seats stand. | | 2 | The Iyi's lineage, and whether the female head's line is the same as the head's or a separate one. | | 3 | The title society's fees, which the sources record at 1972 prices and which are not transferable as they stand. | | 4 | The age of entry to Ozo, and whether the father-bar stays abrogated. | | 5 | The renewal cycle, if the shrine structure is to be rebuilt rather than stand permanently. | | 6 | The intercalary day, and whether the year is thirteen moons exactly. |

And one that was open is now closed. The seminary's name was listed here as open; the author's own book names it — Uko-Ndose — and the training is twelve years, written out in obibi-nso.md Book X, Chapter 2. Odiana keeps the Catholic model of a formed and licensed priesthood, and says that this is an avowed import (canon.md).

The blood ruling, in one place

(The ruling is canon.md A11, and it is the same in every document of this religion.)

An animal is killed at every festival of Odiana and at every serious rite of it. The announcing of the year, the cleansing of a great abomination, the taking of a title, the consecration of a Dibia, the setting of a boundary, the burial of a head, the making of peace, and the opening of a war. The animal is killed in the open, and its blood is spilled upon open ground, away from every holy thing.

And no blood is brought to a shrine, or to an altar, or to a sacred object, or to a tree that is held sacred. Nothing holy in this religion is ever touched with blood. The altar keeps the kola, and the nzu, and the wine, and the water. This is a modernisation of Odinana and it is iwu — made, and published, and dated — and it is not a custom recovered from the ancestors.

What remains bloodless, and stays bloodless:

  • the offering to Chukwu — the tradition's own offering was kola, white chalk and libation, and it is kept;
  • the household shrine — the household oblation is kola, nzu, mmanya and water;
  • the temple altar — no blood is brought to it, ever;
  • the consecration of objects — no shrine, Ofo, Ikenga or medicine is made with blood (canon.md A6);
  • a reading of afa — the reading is free: nothing is charged for it, and the offering is not a fee.

And the one blood that is never shed in this religion, in any rite and for any purpose, is human blood. Where the old practice used a human being, this religion uses the fowl — for it is the fowl that is used in performing sacrifice, and not a human being.

Membership — what makes a person an Odianian

To become an Odianian, one must believe in Ana, the mother earth, for through her does one reach the heart of Chukwu.

This is the one belief required, and the whole of the requirement. A person may come from any town, any house and any tongue, and may know nothing else of this religion. He is not asked to curse the house he came from. He must believe that the ground is alive, and that she remembers what is done upon her, and that through her the heart of Chukwu is reached.

And no one is an Odianian by birth, not because his father was one, and not because he was born in the town. A child born to an Odianian is carried by the household until he is grown enough to answer for himself, and then he makes the profession in his own words.

The rite is Nnabata Odiana — the person stands on bare ground with nothing between his feet and the earth, takes up a handful of the earth, is asked the three questions, and speaks the profession with the earth in his hand. He is marked with nzu, clean water is poured on the ground at his feet, the kola is broken, and the company eats. His name is written in the register of the Ndose, and it records what he professed and not what he was. See Book II Ch.2 for the doctrine of the way, Book VIII Ch.11 for the rite, and Book XVII for the article of the creed.

And one thing is kept absolutely clear, and is not to be blurred: Ana is not Chukwu. She is not the source and not the maker of what has no end. She is the mother, and the way, and the mediator, and is honoured as those are honoured. Whoever worships Ana as though she were Chukwu has made an idol of his own road and has lost the way he was standing on.
